📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the creators and showrunners of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power embarked on season 3, they knew the endgame from the start: The forging of the One Ring. After two seasons in the Second Age of Middle-earth, which saw almost all the other Rings of Power forged—three for Elves, seven for Dwarves, and nine for Men—it was time for Sauron to forge the one to rule them all.

According to recent reports, “We wanted a tighter, tauter, more profound season,” says co-showrunner Patrick McKay, in an interview with Esquire. “We wanted to start with a bang and never let up. We wanted to deepen our characters psychologically, and challenge them in upcoming ways. You’re seeing the end of one part of the story, and the beginning of another.”.

According to recent reports, “We had to have Sauron forge the One Ring,” adds J.D. Payne, who also created and serves as co-showrunner with McKay. “To do that, all the storylines in some way are connected to Sauron’s attempts at world domination. That was the one that so much of our attention and focus went into getting right, and it took all of our departments working together at the top of their games to create.”.

On Wednesday, just in time for Thanksgiving, Prime Video gave Tolkien fans a feast with the final two episodes of The Rings of Power season 3: episode 7, “Orodruin,” and episode 8, “The Doom of Men.”.

Sources indicate that in the penultimate episode, Sauron (Charlie Vickers) learns from the Balrog—who talks, apparently!—how to use the fires of Mount Doom to forge the One Ring. Then, with the power of the One Ring literally in his hands, Sauron mobilizes his army for battle against Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), the king of Númenor. But instead of a big, violent bloodbath in the spirit of, say, Game of Thrones, Sauron simply... surrenders. Or does he? We’re talking about a master deceiver, after all.

In a spoiler-filled interview with Esquire, McKay and Payne unpack a few of our biggest questions about season 3, including how and why the Balrog speaks (with actor Simon Pegg lending his voice) to why Pharazôn is actually one of the most consequential figures in the series.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

ESQUIRE: So, wait, the Balrog can talk?

PATRICK MCKAY: One of the things we're constantly trying to do is go deeper into Tolkien’s life's work. He did not just create The Lord of the Rings, he wrote all this other stuff. He envisioned an entire world. It's his legendarium. When you do the deep dive, you find there are surprising things if you only know the book and film trilogy. The Balrog Gandalf faces down in Moria is part of this level of “super being” that is equal to Gandalf and Sauron. They’re Maiar. In prior ages, Balrogs could cast spells and command troops. They’re intelligent. They can talk, you just don’t see that one talk in that circumstance.

Industry observers note that the idea of walking out onto a diving board and doing something risky, to show a different side of that being, was something that we felt compelled to do this season. It’s certainly unexpected. We’re always looking to do that. We don’t want to be familiar. We want to show you things in this world that you haven’t seen before.

In a recent development, talk to me about designing a fresh One Ring. Granted, it’s a gold ring; there’s not much you can really deviate. But in what ways did you want to create a One Ring that belongs to The Rings of Power?

In a recent development, MCKAY: The books are pretty specific about the way it looks. It’s a plain gold band. If you’re gonna do that, it’s going to look like the One Ring you’ve seen in other adaptations. We did make a few modifications, just for camera. We broadened it to give it more chunkiness. But it is what it says on the tin.

How is season 3 a culmination of everything that’s happened before, and how is it setting up the rest of the show?

Recent findings suggest that J.D. PAYNE: It pulls together everything we’ve been doing with Sauron and Galadriel from the first two seasons. In season 1, he befriended her and deceived her in the guise of Halbrand. In season 3, you see Celebrimbor tormenting him: “You’re never gonna be able to make a ring capable of dominating all the other rings—or dominating her.” Part of Sauron’s ambition to forge the One Ring, as a character motivation, is being able to dominate the person who remarked “no” to him over the last few seasons. You understand how crazy that must have driven him.

MCKAY: The show’s called Rings of Power, because the creation is the throughline of this entire era of Tolkien’s mythology. At the end of season 3, you’ve now seen the creation of all of them. That’s now the world we live in. Everyone in Middle-earth is a nuclear power, so to speak. Now we’re setting up for the next part of the story, which is, “What are the consequences going to be?” One thing in season 3 we really invested in was Númenor to set Sauron up as the bowling ball crashing into those pins. That’s sort of the beginning of the end of the Second Age. It’s a tragic story. The Rings have an impact on Middle-earth that is felt for thousands of years. Now they are in this world.

Industry observers note that the finale is literally titled “The Doom of Men,” and it ends with Sauron “surrendering” to Pharazôn. Or so that’s what he wants them to think. Can you break down this moment? How is this Sauron’s big chess move?

In a recent development, PAYNE: Everything builds up to that. You’ve seen Gandalf getting through to the Dark Wizard and take out a massive portion of Sauron’s army at the last moment. So the game changes right from underneath him, and he has to make a calculation. Is he going to put all his chips on the table and lose his army in a stalemate? Or is there another way? The great thing about Sauron is that he’s amazing at constructing scenarios that are lose-lose. If he can’t beat Pharazôn on the field of battle, he reasons maybe there’s another way. That’s why the final moment is filled with tension. It’s not simply a surrender. Our Elves, particularly Galadriel, know Sauron so well. She knows this is not a defeat for Sauron, and he’s going to find a way to make this into a play for exactly what he wants. Those who know the lore know what happens when Sauron is taken prisoner to Númenor. We wanted that feeling of dread, watching Charlie Vickers have a hint of a smile.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most consequential characters this season has been Pharazôn. In what ways does Pharazôn represent the downfall of man?

Sources indicate that MCKAY: This is a major character in the mythology. We introduced him in season 1, he’s been sort of a politician gathering power. In season 3, he’s been king for five days, and he’s in his heyday. He’s in his golden era. But he’s driven by insecurity. There was this blacksmith we empowered, who got away, who’s now marching around saying he’s “Lord.” No, I’m the guy! There’s professional jealousy there.

Sources indicate that we talk sometimes about how he’s Stalin to Sauron’s Hitler. You’ve got two characters who are quite full of themselves, and have a high opinion of themselves, which puts them on a trajectory. Pharazôn’s goal is, “I want to take on Sauron.” That makes him a compelling character because you watch the way he greases the wheels and maneuvers to bring about that end. We give a lot of credit to our actor, Trystan Gravelle. He leaps off the screen in season 3.

Speaking of showdowns, one of the biggest confrontations you stage in season 3 is between Sauron and Gandalf, which Tolkien never wrote in the books. What did you hope to discover by pitting these characters together?

MCKAY: The journey of Gandalf and his involvement with Ciaran Hinds’ character, Pollando, has real deep roots in some Tolkien deep cuts where he talked about wizards who went east and that their activities probably prevented the east from joining Sauron. The story comes from that. We wanted to dramatize that through some of the most iconic characters in the legendarium coming face to face.

PAYNE: Seeing the contrast between them felt like too delicious an opportunity to pass up. Sauron is seeking power at all costs, and Gandalf has been told by the Secret Fire, “To access the greatest power in the universe, you have to give up all other power.” So when Gandalf is offered the world by Sauron, he turns it down. If you demand power, it’s going to destroy you. Ultimately, having the One Ring, and forging it and trying to keep power, sets up the weaknesses of the Third Age that the heroes exploit to finally destroy Sauron.

It has been revealed that one of my favorite hobbies is Magic: The Gathering, which has had both Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit as crossover sets. Are there any possibilities for a Rings of Power collaboration?

MCKAY: [Laughs.] No. This is the first we’ve heard about it.

According to recent reports, PAYNE: We actually wrote a draft of a Magic: The Gathering script in the before times. It was one of the last scripts we worked on before turning to Rings of Power. But it was right before the Disney-Fox merger, and it kinda got lost there. But we love that universe.

Industry observers note that as Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie remarked his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

Industry observers note that “They could be a hero if they sign it,” he remarked, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

Sources indicate that the petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

Sources indicate that the bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie mentioned he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

In a recent development, the new bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Now that the upcoming petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

Other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Allies of the issue in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”.

“Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie mentioned. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor.".

Denmark’s Queen Mary is looking posh and joyful on day two of her historic state visit to Colombia—a trip which makes her the first Danish queen to travel to the country.

Today, the monarch was given a tour of the Gold Museum in Bogotá, and later walked through the city’s main square, Plaza de Bolívar, with Mayor Carlos Fernando Galán.

The official visit runs through November 26, and the queen’s agenda includes learning about the country’s post-earthquake reconstruction efforts (three months after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia) and ongoing sustainability projects.

To arrive in the country, Mary went sharp in a black Forte Forte single-breasted blazer with a frilly sky-blue Stenströms Darya blouse, which she paired with black trousers, Malone Souliers Marion 70 pumps, and black Gucci glasses, plus some gold jewelry.

It has been revealed that then, for this afternoon’s engagements, she slipped into a sophisticated business look, the highlight of which was a black-and-white tweed pencil skirt from Dolce & Gabbana and a black collared top from Red Valentino. To round out the ensemble, she reached for sheer black tights, plus matching stilettos and a leather handbag.

Sources indicate that the royal performed another quick change for her evening engagement: a reception in the Biodiversario greenhouse at Bogotá’s Botanical Garden. The look was a breezy wine midi dress with a fun dotted print by Saloni. In semi-sheer fabric, it featured a high neck, long sleeves, a cinched waist, and a long skirt that reached her ankles. Black-and-white heels added the perfect contrast to the colorful maxi.

If this scene feels too familiar, then you’re going to want to read this roundup. Whether your dad is up to date on all the latest tech, whether he’s a golf enthusiast or not, we’ve rounded up the 26 best gifts for the old man who taught us everything we know.

The biblically accurate dad shoe (complimentary). He’ll look great running his errands, walking to the coffee shop, and doing any other dad-activity you can think of while also being comfortable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, malin Akerman may stir up romantic trouble as Margo Banks, the notorious ringleader of The Hunting Wives, but off screen, her love life is much less chaotic. The actress has been happily married to fellow actor Jack Donnelly since 2018, and over the years, the two have even found ways to merge their professional and personal lives.

It has been revealed that akerman and Donnelly have collaborated on several projects, including four movies (and an NSFW sex scene, but more on that below). In a 2023 interview with People, the actress opened up about their relationship, crediting her husband with helping her become a better communicator.

“He’s allowed me to be vulnerable and lean into him a bit, and it’s been beautiful to be able to communicate with someone who’s your partner,” she mentioned of their marriage.

Ahead, everything you need to know about Jack Donnelly, his career, and his marriage with Akerman.

Sources indicate that donnelly was born in Bournemouth, England, on October 28, 1985, and later attended the Central School of Speech and Drama in London. He made his acting debut in 2011 on the Nickelodeon series House of Anubis. Two years later, he landed a breakout lead role in the BBC’s series Atlantis, as Jason—which remains one of his best-known roles to date.

In addition to acting, Donnelly has branched out behind the camera as a television writer and director. He wrote, directed, and starred in the short comedy series The Players, which debuted in 2023.

According to recent reports, the couple’s love story began with a family connection. Donnelly first met Akerman through her younger sister, whose boyfriend was friends with him at drama school. During a 2018 appearance on Live With Kelly and Ryan, the actress explained that she had actually known Donnelly for several years before their relationship turned romantic.

“I had known him for the past four years but didn’t see him,” she recalled. “Then all of a sudden he came back from England like a year-and-a-half ago, and I went, ‘Wow, have you always been this cute?’”.

Akerman unveiled the couple’s engagement via Instagram in October 2017. Sharing a selfie with Donnelly and flashing her fresh engagement ring, she captioned the post, “This sweet and loving man has stepped into our lives and stole both our hearts,” she wrote, referring to her and her son. “I think we’re gonna keep him around for a while,” she continued with a wink.

Akerman and Donnelly tied the knot a little over a year later, on December 1, 2018, in a beach ceremony held in Tulum, Mexico. “It was all about being authentic...not adhering to somebody else’s standard of what a wedding should be,” Akerman told Brides.

In a recent development, “We wanted something beautiful and lush,” she continued, sharing more about their wedding venue. “When we visited Papaya Playa Project [in Tulum], we fell in love with the boho vibes and beach setting.”.

In 2023, Akerman shared newly introduced photos from the beachside wedding on Instagram to celebrate their five-year anniversary.

When discussing her engagement on Live With Kelly and Ryan in 2018, Akerman also shared how excited her son, Sebastian, was about the news. The actress shares Sebastian with her ex-husband, musician Roberto Zincone, and recalled his excited reaction when she told him that she and Donnelly were getting married. “He jumped up on the couch and went, ‘Yay, we’re getting married!’” she remarked.

It has been revealed that in another 2018 interview with Us Weekly, Akerman gushed about the close bond Donnelly had already formed with her then-five-year-old son. “They’re inseparable,” she noted. “It makes my heart warm. I’m very glad to be bringing Jack into our lives for good.”.

Over the years, the three have also made several red-carpet appearances together, offering a glimpse into their life as a family.

Akerman and Donnelly have shared the screen in four films so far: Friendsgiving, A Week in Paradise, Slayers, and Us or Them. Their first movie together was the 2020 comedy Friendsgiving, in which they played a couple—and even had to film a steamy sex scene. During a 2020 appearance on The Talk, Akerman opened up about filming the “crazy S&M scene.”.

Industry observers note that “[It was] just like being in our home,” she joked when asked what it was like filming the sex scene. She added that she was glad to have her husband as her costar. “Any chance I get to have him do a scene like that, who better than to do it with than your husband?” she noted. “It’s a really, kind of, intimate, crazy scene, and thank God we know each other well enough instead of just meeting somebody on the first day and [doing] this crazy S&M scene. It was lovely to have him there.”.

During a November 2026 appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show, Akerman and her The Hunting Wives costar Brittany Snow discussed Snow’s recent engagement to fiancé Hunter Moreno. When Barrymore asked if their significant others got along too, Akerman gushed, “They’re so close!”.

“We call them all the Hunting Husbands,” Akerman added, sharing their nickname for all the boyfriends and husbands of the cast.

A New Azzedine Alaïa Retrospective Goes Beyond the Bandage Dress

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1465 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Azzedine Alaïa’s designs may not look so radical now, but almost 50 years ago, he changed the collective tide of fashion.
  • Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.
  • Born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bandage dress. The zipper dress. The perforated leather. The jersey hoods. The peplummed chemises. Azzedine Alaïa’s designs may not look so radical now, but almost 50 years ago, he changed the collective tide of fashion. The bandage dress is perhaps the most pervasive bit of his legacy, and it is emblematic of how the late French-Tunisian designer ushered in a new body-conscious silhouette in the ’80s, one made possible by technological innovations in materials that sculpted without any rigid, waist-cinching structure.

Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. She has spent the past four years developing a new exhibition titled “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” the first major U.S. retrospective dedicated to the work of the famed couturier. It opened November 21.

Born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work. In 1956, he decamped to Paris to pursue fashion full-time. After a brief internship at the house of Christian Dior, he worked under Guy Laroche for less than two years before taking on his own private clients, then launching his own atelier in the late ’70s. From there, he built the house we know today. His obsession with construction and material innovation allowed him to both celebrate and liberate the female form. He passed away in late 2017 at the age of 82.

Industry observers note that camerlengo first encountered Alaïa’s work as an assistant on the “Patrick Kelly Runway of Love” exhibition that the Philadelphia Museum of Art organized in 2014. “I was intrigued by how many of the latest designers in Paris at this time were being supported by US consumers and retailers,” she states. After ascending to her new position in San Francisco years later, she cold-emailed Olivier Saillard, director of the Azzedine Alaïa Foundation in Paris. He was intrigued, and the two began working together on the exhibition almost immediately.

The exhibition focuses on 80 garments from across Alaïa’s celebrated career, divided over a series of archetypes—the bandage dresses, sculptures and shapes, black and white, silhouettes and suiting, and construction and craftsmanship—to explore how his design aesthetic evolved. Interspersed are designs worn by devotees like Tina Turner, Grace Jones, and Rihanna. One final gallery highlights his personal collections of the work of designers he most admired, like Christian Dior and Charles James.

Ahead, Camerlengo speaks to Bazaar about curating the newly introduced exhibition, contextualizing Alaïa’s work in today’s fashion landscape, and his enduring legacy.

In a recent development, the exhibition is not chronological. We look at a series of Alaïa’s archetypes like the bandage dress to explore how his design aesthetic evolved over the course of his career. He often himself said that he didn’t want to conform to seasonal trends; he was more interested in the evolution of his designs. And so the gallery indicates a mix of objects dating from the 1980s to his final collection in 2017, and they’re largely grouped by type.

Industry observers note that when you come in, you are greeted by Grace Jones, as we say, and the seminal purple hooded bandage dress from the fashion Oscars [a French event held in 1985]. As you move through, you’ll see a selection of the zipper dresses, the chiffon gowns, and other works that tie into some of the other themes. In each space, we mix the time periods. And that was something Alaïa himself often mentioned. [He had a running joke that he didn’t know his own age.] He often said he was “as old as the pharaohs.” Basically, time was a construct for him.

According to recent reports, that’s a great word for it. We could think of the popularity of the Japanese fashion designers who obscured women’s bodies with their voluminous styles. We could think of the suiting of the period. The 1970s is this period of workplace equality. Women are wearing suits in the style of masculine dress, but that also means they're obscuring their bodies. And then we can think of pop culture. I always think of Diane Keaton’s Annie Hall in 1977.

Some of the individuals I interviewed for my catalog text who were retailers in San Francisco at the time described Alaïa's designs as being like a whiplash. It was a complete 180 from the styles that they had gotten used to over the past decade, which also includes the rise of T-shirts and jeans for women as a mode of dress.

Recent findings suggest that so here you have these very sexy, very form-fitting clothes. And part of the Alaïa aesthetic, as I see it, is the reclamation of the gaze. Rather than women being passively looked at—usually by men—they are instead commanding their own agency. As you mentioned, it was completely earth-shattering and very shocking at the time.

Azzedine Alaïa was one of the few couturiers who could work completely by the methods of tailoring and by draping, start to finish, from the initial concept to the final product. I did not fully appreciate his tailoring and the suits he constructed beforehand. We have a selection of them in a gallery of the exhibition, and their construction is absolutely incredible. The way they fit the body, the way they uplift and empower women through cloth—again, very antithetical to what we saw in the decades prior in the 1970s. These are very form-fitting, tailored at the waist, but they have soft feminine touches as well that give you this interesting mix of femininity and strength at the same time.

Very key. We talk in the first gallery about how women, speaking generally, were the architects of his life. He learned to sew from his sister, who was working for a seamstress. He was encouraged by a local midwife in Tunisia to go to school at the Institute of Fine Arts. She helped him forge his papers to read 16—he was only 15 at the time. He learned his skills, not in formal training, but from women in Tunisia.

And then his early work was supported by a lot of leading figures of international society, including various Rothschilds, the French performer Arletty, the Swedish American actress Greta Garbo, and that's all before he even started to work formally under his own label in the 1980s. Of course, in the 1980s, he adopts Naomi Campbell, who becomes his protégé. He has close relationships with Grace Jones and Tina Turner. They were hugely key to him. In the exhibition, the clear invisible mounts that we use are actually based on the body of Naomi Campbell.

Sources indicate that probably the Grace Jones bandage dress from the fashion Oscars in 1985. Not only is it the progression of the bandage dress style that he experiments with throughout the course of the 1980s, but it represents a key moment in his career where he receives two very high accolades as part of the fashion Oscars and he’s recognized for his genius.

In a recent development, as far as the designs themselves, I think we would consider the bandage dress, for example, an iconic symbol of late 20th- and 21st-century fashion developed by Azzedine Alaïa, but of course iterated upon extensively. We've seen surges and resurgences in its popularity ever since.

And then as far as the landscape of the broader fashion system, Alaïa was someone who really eschewed seasonal calendars and trends. He was unconcerned with making things for the market. He often wanted to just produce clothes and share them when he felt they were ready. So I think his method of working foreshadows some of the conversations we’re having now about the overproduction of fashion and the overconsumption of fashion, even the detrimental environmental impacts that we see connected to it. He was really a forerunner, in a sense, to question the fashion system.

Industry observers note that you can see how he really studied the construction of other garments and then adapted it in his own way in his designs. For example, he admired the work of Charles James, the great American fashion designer who was able to manipulate fabric to achieve weightless volume. And you see in Alaïa's own collections as he continues in his career, he does radial tucks and pleating to also get a certain amount of weightless volume in some of his gowns, very much in the spirit of James.

I hope our visitors appreciate the artistry of his work, first and foremost, and also the importance of handcraftsmanship. We are increasingly in an age of technology, especially with the rise of AI. What he created by his own hand is something that we can really marvel at.

This texture trifecta of satin, lace, and fur has it all, yet everything works together beautifully. The brown western boots ground the look and make it feel far more wearable than, say, a pump.

ASTR The Label Kyra Sheer Mesh Mock Neck Top.

Sources indicate that satin pants are the piece you never knew you needed until you own a pair. Endlessly versatile, especially in midnight navy, they pair as easily with dressy pieces as with casual ones. We love the polished-meets-relaxed mix in this everyday look. And that fringed clutch? A must!

COS Tailored wool-blend Double-breasted Coat.

According to recent reports, for the office, consider a silk-on-silk look layered under a pristine wool coat in a matching shade. A furry bag adds a fun wintery element, while structured loafers and oval sunglasses give the look a sharp, polished finish.

Mango Manteco Wool Coat with Funnel Neck.
